summaries.gardner: Marriott is the top dog of global lodging (10,082 properties and 1.81 million rooms at June 30, 2026) with strong momentum (shares up 43.6% over 52 weeks), but it is a mature franchising business growing revenue about 4% a year rather than an emerging-industry rule breaker. Its brands and the 295-million-member Bonvoy program are well known, and the stock's 40x trailing P/E draws 'expensive' comments, which Gardner would not mind.
summaries.buffett: Marriott fits several Buffett traits: a simple, asset-light fee business, consistent cash generation (free cash flow of about $2.6 billion in 2025, roughly equal to net income of $2,601M) and steady buybacks that cut diluted shares from 325.8 million in 2022 to 273.6 million in 2025. Against that, it relies on $16.9 billion of debt, carries a stockholders' deficit, and at about 41 times 2025 EPS the price leaves little room for error.
summaries.munger: Inverting, the main failure paths are a deep travel recession or shock like 2020 (when Marriott lost $267M), owners defecting to rival brands, and leverage. The brand-and-loyalty network makes the franchise durable, but Munger's 'great business at a fair price' test is strained by a trailing P/E near 41.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would call Marriott a stalwart: a big, well-known company with EPS that tripled from $3.15 in 2015 to $9.51 in 2025, helped by buybacks. But with a forward P/E of about 32 against high-single to mid-teens EPS growth, the PEG of about 2.6 is well above Lynch's preferred level and the stock is widely followed by 29 analysts.
summaries.fisher: Marriott scores well on Fisher's sales and franchise-building points, with a 629,000-room pipeline and new co-brand card deals with JPMorgan Chase and American Express, but it does little R&D in the classic sense. Management depth and long-term owner relationships are strengths; margins are steady rather than expanding.
summaries.graham: Marriott fails Graham's defensive tests: it lost money in 2020, suspended its dividend from 2020 to 2022, trades at about 41 times trailing earnings and has negative book value. It is large and its EPS has grown strongly over ten years, but there is no margin of safety in Graham's sense.
summaries.thiel: Marriott is not a Zero to One company: it has no breakthrough technology and competes in a mature industry with Hilton, Hyatt, IHG and Accor. Its strength is scale and distribution through Bonvoy and franchise relationships, a durable but not monopolistic position.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price with operating discipline; Marriott shows the discipline (asset-light model, $4.5 billion-plus of planned 2026 capital returns) but revenue growth of about 4% and a forward P/E near 32 make it neither a high-growth compounder nor cheap.
summaries.druckenmiller: Momentum is strong (up 43.6% in a year versus 14.2% for SPY) and full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance was raised to $5,965M-$6,025M, but Q3 guidance of $2.74-$2.82 adjusted EPS came in below the $2.93 consensus and Middle East RevPAR fell 43% in Q2. Liquidity and travel demand drive results, so it is a cyclical rather than a high-conviction liquidity play.
summaries.smith: Marriott has Terry Smith-style qualities: a capital-light franchise with return on invested capital around 16% and cash conversion near 100% of net income. But it is cyclical, leveraged and, at a free-cash-flow yield of about 2.7%, arguably overpriced by Smith's 'don't overpay' rule.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Marriott's return on capital is good but its earnings yield is low: EV of about $119 billion against 2025 operating income of $4,141M gives roughly 3.5%. It would not rank near the top of a Greenblatt screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three legs: the business is good (asset-light fees, ROIC about 16%), management is shareholder-minded (heavy buybacks, family influence through roughly 9% insider ownership), but reinvestment opportunities are limited because growth comes from owners' capital and most cash is returned. The stool is strong on two legs and weak on reinvestment.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks low-risk, high-uncertainty bets at deep discounts; Marriott is a well-understood, fully priced stock at about 41 times trailing earnings, so there is no Dhandho-style mispricing despite the business's resilience.
summaries.wood: Marriott is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator; it is an incumbent hospitality franchisor, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomics.
summaries.ackman: Marriott resembles the simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, high-barrier businesses Ackman favours (he has owned Hilton), with a dominant brand portfolio and asset-light fees. It meets the quality bar, though at the current price the valuation upside is limited.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model fits partly: Marriott's growing system and 295-million-member Bonvoy program lower distribution costs for owners and make it harder for independents to compete. But it does not visibly pass savings to guests the way Costco or Amazon do, and much of its cash goes to buybacks rather than reinvestment.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed huge, fast-growing markets with technical founders; Marriott is a mature hospitality company growing about 4% a year, so it does not fit Sequoia's venture lens.
summaries.nash: Marriott fails several of Nash's hard filters: revenue grew only 4.3% in 2025, operating margin was 15.8%, and debt ($16.9 billion) far exceeds cash ($462M). Its quality traits (moat, loyalty, momentum, 5-year outperformance) are strong, but the DCF and PEG tests point to a stretched valuation.

momentum.evidence: MAR closed at $390.71 on Oct 23, 2026, up 43.61% over 52 weeks (StockAnalysis), against a 14.23% one-year total return for SPY.

g4.evidence: CEO Anthony Capuano (CEO since February 2021) has a long Marriott career and the Marriott family still holds about 9% of shares, but no famous outside investor champions the stock.

g6.evidence: At a trailing P/E of about 41 and above the $387.77 average analyst target, some commentators call it expensive, though the consensus rating is still Buy.

simple.evidence: Marriott earns franchise, management and incentive fees from 10,082 hotels and passes owners' costs through as reimbursements, a model a generalist can follow.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $10,571M in 2020 to $26,186M in 2025, but the business lost $267M in 2020 and is exposed to travel cycles.

integrity.evidence: Management reports candidly and has returned capital steadily ($3,300M of buybacks and $718M of dividends in 2025), but leverage has risen and the Marriott family retains significant influence.

b6.evidence: Marriott has grown by acquisition (Starwood in 2016, City Express in 2022 for $100M), though recent deals have been small and capital light.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 16% (StockAnalysis), but the company runs with a $3,771M stockholders' deficit and $16.9 billion of debt.

fcf.evidence: 2025 operating cash flow of $3,212M less $604M of capital and technology spending gave about $2,608M of free cash flow, roughly equal to net income of $2,601M.

b10.evidence: Despite heavy buybacks, retained capital has compounded value: diluted EPS rose from $3.15 in 2015 to $9.51 in 2025 and the share price has more than doubled over five years.

safety.evidence: A simple DCF using Marriott's own three-year averages gives roughly $87 per share at a 12% discount rate, far below the $390.71 price.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 41, forward P/E of 31.7 and PEG of 2.63 are high for revenue growth of about 4% and EPS growth in the mid-teens.

mu5.evidence: The business has few ways to fail permanently thanks to its brand scale, but 2020 showed a travel shock can erase profits and leverage adds risk.

reinvest.evidence: Growth needs little capital because owners fund hotels (capex $604M in 2025), so most cash is returned rather than reinvested at high rates.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart: a large, steady fee-based hotel franchisor growing rooms about 4.5-5% a year and buying back shares.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E of about 41 far exceeds the guided 16-18% adjusted EPS growth for 2026.

runway.evidence: A 629,000-room pipeline and net rooms growth guided at the low end of 4.5-5% give years of steady unit growth, but not rapid sales growth.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 325.8 million in 2022 to 264.5 million in Q2 2026, but no notable insider open-market buying was found.

ly8.evidence: Marriott is covered by 29 analysts and is a widely held large cap.

fi2.evidence: Marriott keeps adding brands and products, including the City Express midscale acquisition and new co-brand credit card deals with JPMorgan Chase and American Express.

fi3.evidence: Marriott does not report R&D spending; its technology spending is folded into capital and technology expenditures.

fi4.evidence: Its development team keeps signing deals, with a pipeline of about 629,000 rooms, and Bonvoy has more than 295 million members.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in loyalty and technology platforms, but returns most cash via buybacks (over $4.5 billion planned for 2026).
